clinicalPearls: A hair-shaft disorder in which hairs show regular beading, with elliptical nodes and narrowed internodes, and fracture at the constrictions
Presents with sparse, short, brittle hair and patchy alopecia, often with prominent follicular keratosis (keratosis pilaris), especially on the occiput and nape
Onset is typically in infancy or early childhood after normal lanugo is shed
Most cases are autosomal dominant due to mutations in hair-cortex keratin genes (KRT81, KRT83, KRT86); a recessive form is caused by DSG4 mutations
Diagnosis is confirmed by light microscopy of hair showing the characteristic beaded (moniliform) shafts
Severity varies and some improvement may occur with age, during summer, or in pregnancy
Management is supportive with gentle hair care, emollients/keratolytics for follicular hyperkeratosis, and avoidance of trauma; oral retinoids have been tried in severe cases
reference.pathophysiology: Monilethrix is usually an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the type II hair-cortex keratin genes KRT81, KRT83 and KRT86; a rarer autosomal recessive form results from mutations in DSG4 encoding desmoglein 4. These genes are essential for normal assembly of the keratin intermediate-filament network and cell adhesion within the hair cortex. The mutations produce periodic weakness along the hair shaft, giving alternating nodes (of normal calibre) and internodes (constricted, medulla-deficient segments). The narrowed internodes are mechanically fragile and fracture readily, so hairs break before reaching any length, producing the clinical picture of short, sparse, brittle hair with follicular hyperkeratosis.
additionalDifferentials: Keratosis pilaris atrophicans / other follicular keratoses with alopecia
additionalInvestigations: Light microscopy of plucked or cut hairs showing regular beading
Trichoscopy (dermoscopy) demonstrating the regularly bent, beaded shafts
Molecular genetic testing of KRT81, KRT83, KRT86 and DSG4
Scalp examination for follicular keratosis and pattern of alopecia
Skin biopsy of scalp where the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Extensive alopecia causing significant psychosocial distress
Associated features suggesting a broader ectodermal or syndromic disorder
Secondary infection or inflammation of hyperkeratotic follicles
Atypical hair-shaft findings prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Monilethrix is a chronic condition, but it is compatible with normal health and often improves spontaneously with age, in summer months, or during pregnancy. Complete resolution is uncommon and hair fragility tends to persist, though severity fluctuates.
pitfalls: Mistaking the alopecia for alopecia areata or tinea and missing the diagnostic hair-shaft beading
Failing to examine hairs microscopically, which is the key diagnostic step
Confusing genuine monilethrix with artefactual pseudomonilethrix
Aggressive cosmetic or chemical hair treatment that worsens breakage
management: Gentle hair care to minimise mechanical fracture at the constricted internodes, avoiding traction, vigorous brushing, heat styling and chemical treatments
A trial of topical minoxidil, which can improve hair growth and length in some patients
Topical keratolytics such as urea or salicylic acid, emollients and topical retinoids for the associated follicular keratosis
Reassurance that the disorder is compatible with normal health and often improves with age, during summer months or in pregnancy
Trichoscopy and light microscopy of hair shafts to confirm the diagnosis and monitor severity over time
Genetic counselling addressing the usual autosomal dominant hair-cortex keratin inheritance and the rarer autosomal recessive DSG4 form, with assessment of affected relatives
